title: GeoJSON Centroid Calculator: Mean Centre
description: Calculate the mean coordinate centre across a GeoJSON object's vertices with the GeoJSON Centroid Calculator — quick dataset orientation. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a four-feature sample around New York centres at 40.7298, −73.9397 — the vertex average, sitting between its Times Square point and its JFK point, exactly as a mean should.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Centroid Calculator computes the mean coordinate centre across all vertices in a GeoJSON object — a fast orientation point for a dataset. Paste the GeoJSON and read the centre — the average of every coordinate pair, vertex-mean nature stated plainly.

body.t: Open the map where the data’s weight sits. The vertex mean is a better default than a capital city — and the
supplies the zoom’s frame around it.
One coordinate summarising a file travels well in catalogues and tickets: ‘the dataset centred at…’ orients anyone in one line.
This month’s centre versus last month’s quantifies drift — coverage creeping, sensors migrating, territories shifting.
A file that should centre on Ohio but centres on the Atlantic has swapped or unsigned coordinates. The centroid is the fastest liar-catcher after the bbox.

A file with one detailed coastline polygon (10,000 vertices) and one city point centres near the coastline — the mean counts vertices, not features. That is the method, stated: detailed geometry outvotes sparse geometry.

A polygon’s true centre of mass can sit far from its vertices’ mean when vertices cluster along one intricate shore. This calculator is explicit about being the vertex mean; polygon-mass centroids are a different, heavier computation.

popular_table.note: The method note is the product: a vertex mean is honest for orientation and fingerprints. Publications needing a defensible ‘centre of the region’ should compute the area-weighted centroid in GIS.

faq: No — deliberately and openly. Every vertex counts once. Densely-digitised geometry pulls the centre toward itself; the examples on this page show the effect so it never surprises you.
The mean of the points — identical in spirit to the CSV centroid. A points file is the method’s home turf.
Hole vertices are vertices — they vote. For most files their pull is negligible; for a donut metropolis it is part of the dataset’s shape.

Arithmetic longitude averaging breaks at the seam (179 and −179 average to 0). Pacific-centred files should be seam-shifted before averaging — the calculator reports the naive mean and the caveat stands here in writing.
Displayed to five decimals; the honest uncertainty is the dataset’s spread, typically far larger. A centre is a summary, not a survey mark.
They contribute no vertices and no votes; a file with no coordinates at all has no centre, reported as such.
Can I use it as a label point?
For orientation graphics, yes; for guaranteed inside-the-polygon labels, no — means can fall outside concave shapes (a crescent’s mean sits in its bay). Label points are their own GIS craft.
